## Reasoning

At each boundary, two adjacent phases coexist, so I set ΔG = 0 for the reaction converting one phase to the other (consuming ½O₂). With O₂ at pressure *p*, the reaction free energy is ΔG = ΔG° − ½RT ln(p), giving **ln(p) = 2ΔG°/(RT)**.

**Boundary a — Fe/FeO:** Fe + ½O₂ → FeO
$$\ln p_a = \frac{2\Delta G^\circ_{\text{FeO}}}{RT} = \frac{2(-206.95\times10^3)}{8.314\times1000} = -49.78$$

**Boundary b — FeO/Fe₃O₄:** 3FeO + ½O₂ → Fe₃O₄
$$\Delta G^\circ = \Delta G^\circ_{\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4} - 3\Delta G^\circ_{\text{FeO}} = -792.6 + 620.85 = -171.75\text{ kJ}$$
$$\ln p_b = \frac{2(-171.75\times10^3)}{RT} = -41.32$$

**Boundary c — Fe₃O₄/Fe₂O₃:** 2Fe₃O₄ + ½O₂ → 3Fe₂O₃
$$\Delta G^\circ = 3\Delta G^\circ_{\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3} - 2\Delta G^\circ_{\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4} = -1685.4 + 1585.2 = -100.2\text{ kJ}$$
$$\ln p_c = \frac{2(-100.2\times10^3)}{RT} = -24.11$$

The computed pressures satisfy the expected ordering $p_a < p_b < p_c$, confirming the stability sequence Fe → FeO → Fe₃O₄ → Fe₂O₃ with increasing oxygen pressure.
